verdict.rationale: James 5:14-16 sets healing inside a petition frame addressed to the present church: the sick one calls the elders (presbyterous) who pray (proseuxasthosan, aorist imperative) and anoint with oil (aleipsantes elaio), and the prayer of faith will save (sosei) the sick one and the Lord will raise (egerei, with kyrios as the explicit subject) him up. James 5:16 then commands mutual prayer that you may be healed (iathete, aorist passive subjunctive of iaomai). 1 Cor 12:9, 28, 30 lists charismata iamaton (gifts of healings, plural) among the Spirit's ongoing distributions to the church. Acts 28:8-9 narrates Paul praying and laying hands on Publius's father so that the man is healed (iasato), and the rest of the island then keep being cured (etherapeuonto, imperfect). The same canon also limits the claim: Paul prays three times for the thorn and is answered with grace not removal (2 Cor 12:8-9), leaves Trophimus sick (2 Tim 4:20), and prescribes wine for Timothy's frequent illnesses (1 Tim 5:23). The combined lexical pattern affirms that God can and sometimes does heal in answer to prayer while withholding any guarantee.

scripture.force: Is any among you sick (asthenei tis en hymin). Let him call (proskalesastho, aorist imperative) the elders of the church, and let them pray over him (proseuxasthosan ep auton, aorist imperative plural), anointing him with oil (aleipsantes elaio) in the name of the Lord. The grammar is petition and ministry by the gathered assembly directed toward a sovereign healer. The verb proseuxasthosan plus the prepositional phrase ep auton frames healing as something asked of God on behalf of the sick, not a self-executing technique.

And the prayer of faith will save (sosei, future active indicative) the sick one (ton kamnonta), and the Lord will raise (egerei, future active with ho kyrios as explicit subject) him up. The healing is predicated of the Lord as agent, and the following kan (and if he has committed sins) attaches forgiveness as a conditional outcome, showing the verse describes God acting in mercy through prayer rather than asserting an unconditional promise that every prayer secures bodily cure.

Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another (euchesthe hyper allelon, present imperative) that you may be healed (iathete, aorist passive subjunctive of iaomai in a hopos purpose clause). The passive plus subjunctive marks healing as a divinely granted result of prayer, not a mechanical consequence. The closing summary, the prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective (polu ischyei deesis dikaiou energoumene), locates the power in God's response to answered prayer.

To another gifts of healings (charismata iamaton) by the one Spirit. Paul lists healing among the charismata distributed by the Spirit to the assembled body, parallel with faith, prophecy, tongues, and the discernment of spirits. The plural iamaton is significant. Healing is plural and various, not a single guaranteed result, and the verb verse 11 supplies (diairoun idia hekasto kathos bouletai) attributes the distribution to the Spirit's own will.

God placed (etheto ho theos) in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers (dynameis), then gifts of healings (charismata iamaton). The aorist etheto locates the placement of these gifts in the church (en te ekklesia), and the categories sit in a list given to the standing assembly, not bracketed to the apostles alone.

The father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in, prayed (proseuxamenos, aorist participle), laid hands on him (epitheis tas cheiras), and healed him (iasato auton, aorist middle of iaomai with the apostle as the immediate subject and the verb of healing as the explicit outcome). Verse 9 then reports that the rest of the sick on the island came and were being healed (etherapeuonto, imperfect, durative). The narrative supplies an instance in which prayer accompanied healing as an actual event.

Concerning this thing I implored the Lord three times (hyper toutou tris ton kyrion parekalesa) that it might depart (apostei) from me. A repeated, earnest petition for relief is recorded, establishing that the apostle himself prayed for his own healing.

The answer is arkei soi he charis mou (my grace is sufficient for you), with he gar dynamis en astheneia teleitai (for power is perfected in weakness). The petition for removal is explicitly not granted. God answers with grace rather than cure, which directly establishes that healing in answer to prayer is not guaranteed even for an apostle.

Trophimon de apelipon en Mileto asthenounta (I left Trophimus sick at Miletus). An apostle traveling with healing gifts leaves a companion ill rather than curing him, confirming that bodily healing was not dispensed on demand and was not an automatic outcome.

Use a little wine for your stomach and your frequent illnesses (dia ton stomachon kai tas pyknas sou astheneias). The prescription of an ordinary remedy for chronic sickness, given by an apostle to a co-worker, shows that miraculous healing was not assumed to be guaranteed and that natural means coexist with prayer.

The signs of the apostle (ta semeia tou apostolou) were worked out among you in all endurance, by signs and wonders and powers (semeiois te kai terasin kai dynamesin). The vocabulary marks an authenticating function of miracles tied to apostleship, which a cessationist lens treats as a clue that the apostolic-era miraculous concentration does not directly transfer. The same text does not, however, supply a clause forbidding ordinary prayer for healing.

complicating_texts.resolution: Read in isolation the prayer of faith will save the sick (sosei) could be pressed into an unconditional guarantee of bodily cure. The grammar resists this. The Lord is the explicit subject of egerei (will raise), making healing his act of mercy, and the surrounding canon (2 Cor 12:8-9, 2 Tim 4:20, 1 Tim 5:23) shows that earnest prayer for healing is sometimes answered by sustaining grace or left to ordinary means. The verse therefore affirms that God heals in answer to prayer without promising it in every case.

This text could be read as denying that God heals through prayer at all. The lexical force is narrower. A specific petition for removal was answered with sufficient grace, which presupposes that the petition was heard and that God could have granted it. It limits the claim of a guarantee but does not contradict that God can and sometimes does heal.

Ta semeia tou apostolou pairs miraculous signs with apostolic credentialing and gives a cessation-leaning reading a real foothold. The text limits the proposition that all apostolic-era manifestations transfer unchanged. It does not, on the words themselves, cancel the standing James 5 directive to call the elders, pray, and anoint. The proposition under test is the lower-bar claim that God can and sometimes does heal in answer to prayer, which 2 Cor 12:12 does not deny.

Me pantes charismata echousin iamaton (do not all have gifts of healings) expects the answer no. This forecloses the strong continuationist claim that every believer carries a healing gift, but it presupposes the very category by name. It supports the open proposition (the gift exists in the church) while denying universality.

variants.note: James and the Pauline epistles fall outside the 3 John CBGM sample so the variant assessment is shadow only. The apparatus marks visible in the bundle (editorial sigla in Jas 5:14-16 and 2 Cor 12:7-9) touch word order, the connective oun, and pronoun spelling, none of which alter the petition-and-sovereign-outcome pattern that grounds the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: James 5:14-16 commands the present church to call elders, pray, anoint, and confess so that the sick may be healed (iathete). 1 Cor 12:9, 28, 30 names charismata iamaton (gifts of healings) among the Spirit's distributions to the church without a textual time-stamp limiting them. Acts 28:8 narrates iasato (he healed) following prayer and laying on of hands. The lexical pattern is dense and the verbs are present-tense imperatives addressed to the assembly.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: limits the claim but does not contradict it on the words alone
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Ta semeia tou apostolou (2 Cor 12:12) couples signs and powers with the apostolic role, and the New Testament records apostolic-era healings concentrated around the foundational mission (Acts 3, 5, 9, 19, 28). The same canon shows Paul's own petitions for healing met with grace not cure (2 Cor 12:8-9), Trophimus left sick (2 Tim 4:20), and Timothy's chronic illness answered with wine (1 Tim 5:23). On the words alone, the canon supplies no explicit clause canceling the James 5 directive to pray, so a strict cessation of all healing prayer would require an inference the text does not state. The cessationist lens is therefore strongest as a limit on the SCOPE and FUNCTION of miraculous healing, not as a denial of the lower-bar claim that God still hears and sometimes answers prayer for healing.

A reading that takes Jas 5:15 sosei as an absolute promise of bodily cure cannot account for the Lord being the explicit agent of egerei, the conditional kan clause attached to forgiveness, the rhetorical me pantes (1 Cor 12:30) that explicitly denies universality of the healing gift, or 2 Cor 12:8-9, 2 Tim 4:20, and 1 Tim 5:23, where sincere prayer for healing is met with grace, departure, or ordinary remedy.

hermeneutics.notes: The two live lenses are continuationism and cessationism. The proposition under test is the lower-bar open claim (God can and sometimes does heal), which sits below the disputed point that divides the two lenses (whether the New Testament healing charismata still operate as gifts in the present church). Both lenses can affirm the open claim on its own words. The verdict therefore is robust across the live divide.

stem_audit.notes: The proposition is already balanced (God can and sometimes does heal, healing is a sovereign mercy, not a guaranteed outcome) and does not smuggle in a tradition-specific verdict. It neither asserts guaranteed healing nor cessation. It must be distinguished from the parallel false proposition prc-healing-in-atonement-guaranteed, which would press iaomai in Isa 53:5 / 1 Pet 2:24 into a guarantee of bodily cure in the atonement. The present stem makes the weaker open claim, and the lexical data reads cleanly against the plain stem.

lay_summary: James tells a sick believer to call the elders, who pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. The verbs for praying and anointing are commands aimed at God, and the promise that follows says the prayer of faith will save the sick and that the Lord will raise him up. The healing verb has the Lord as its subject, so the help is something God does, not a result the ritual forces. James then commands mutual prayer so that you may be healed, where the verb for healed is passive, marking healing as a hoped-for divine result of prayer rather than an automatic outcome. The same writer Paul lists gifts of healings, in the plural, among the Spirit's distributions to the church, and Acts records Paul praying for the sick father of Publius and the man being healed, with more sick people on the island then being healed afterward. The rest of the New Testament fills in the other half of the picture. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be taken away, and the answer was not removal but the words my grace is sufficient for you. Paul left his coworker Trophimus sick at Miletus rather than curing him, and he told Timothy to take a little wine for a weak stomach and frequent illnesses. Paul also reminds the Corinthians of the signs of the apostle, which gives a reader leaning toward cessation a real foothold by tying signs and powers to the apostolic office. Putting these texts side by side, the words on the page support exactly what the question states. God can heal and sometimes does heal when his people pray, and the language treats that healing as a gift from a sovereign Lord. At the same time the same writers record prayers for healing that were answered with grace rather than cure, and a rhetorical question that expects the answer no when it asks whether all believers have gifts of healings. So the texts give no guarantee that every request for healing will be granted, and they leave room for the live disagreement over whether the apostolic-era concentration of miraculous healing carries forward in the same form, while still affirming the lower-bar claim that healing remains a real mercy available in answer to prayer.
